segments.title: THE CHART THAT GOES BLANK
segments.angle: Imagine this idea has been implemented and failed spectacularly one year from now. What are the most likely reasons for its failure? How could we mitigate those risks now?

sources.text: Consistency Compounds Exponentially: Allowing your consistency to break sets you back magnitudes more than you could ever imagine.
Staying On Your Purpose: Spend at least 1 hour a day doing what you feel you're meant to do, now.
Staying On Your Purpose: Don't wait any longer.

Consistency Compounds Exponentially: Every time you choose to do something other than following your routine, you've just nipped your opportunity for compounding growth at its bud, before it's even had a chance to grow.
Staying On Your Purpose: Don't believe the myth that "one day, things will be different". They won't.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: In the small hours the kettle's ticking up toward the boil. Your eyes land on the mug on its tile. You'll start properly tomorrow, and the purpose note has a name for that sentence: a myth. Here it comes anyway.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Most people think a missed day is just a missed day. One slipped session, one bad week, and the plan's still in the drawer, barely dented. I'd have believed that too.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Barely dented? The note hears the first crack in a dam. A slip is never only a slip, March. It is the opening, and the water does not wait for permission.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So you're saying one missed morning is how the whole plan falls over.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Almost. The missed hour is only the crack. What brings the wall down is the story you tell afterward. The note puts it plainly: 'Allowing your consistency to break sets you back magnitudes more than you could ever imagine.' The best of what it says about the story I am keeping back for later.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the hour itself is nothing. It's what you decide the day after.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Precisely. The hour is nothing. The sum you were building is everything, and you were the one who allowed it to break.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fair. Anyway, the mug.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Let's say it's a year from now and the plan's dead.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Dead already? How swift.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Autopsy time. The routine was an hour before the kettle, set for a good morning. Then a cold morning arrives, the hour's impossible, and you stay under the blanket.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Next day you open the chart. There's a gap in it. The streak's broken, so why bother. The kettle stays cold, and the brass key goes back in the wrong pocket.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Laziness, March. Plain idleness. The man simply could not be bothered.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Could he? Or did one gap make the whole plan look like a lie? From outside it's idleness. From inside it looks finished, so there's no point.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A romantic reading. Lazy men have always had better stories.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ha. Please.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So what would the stool have been that day? Not the full hour. A kettle and one try at the key. One foot, one try at the lock.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A pitiful gesture. A stool is no match for a streak already broken.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's the only thing keeping the run alive.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Sentimental, and quite dreadful.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now, March, I must ask what you hid in the design. You keep a part of yourself out of the room. I have a theory. The moth on the lamp. You are the moth, drawn in and sure to singe. Yes?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: No, the moth is nowhere near...

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the loose coat-hook screw. You are that screw, always working free of the wall just when...

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Wrong. And you're hunting for a rule.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The dimmer, then. A secret switch that lowers you when no one is looking.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nope. You're enjoying this far too much.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Enjoying? I am enduring a long, dreary list of refusals. Must you rule them out one by one, March? It is dreadfully long.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Guilty, and you're still guessing.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You keep guessing, and I keep knocking them down. Here's why it matters. You just built a plan with a hidden part, sitting where nobody checks. That's how a routine fails too. Quietly, somewhere nobody's looking.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Very well. Quiet failures, both of them, and I concede that much.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Now set the purpose note beside it. 'Spend at least 1 hour a day doing what you feel you're meant to do, now.' And the blunt one: 'Don't wait any longer.'

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The consistency note says never let the chain break. The purpose note says do the hour now. Side by side, they catch each other out.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Go on. What do they catch?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A trap. An all or nothing streak makes one missed day feel like ruin, and ruin is the easiest excuse to quit. So you wait for a perfect week, and the perfect week never shows up.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So the chain itself is the snare. Never break it, and any break becomes a verdict.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Exactly.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Yes. The safe version is the smallest one you can keep on a bad day. Not the full hour. The stool.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Neither note shows that alone. One demands a perfect record, the other demands action now. Only together do they admit the perfect record is what kills the action.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So imagine someone who believes the all or nothing version. Their streak chart goes blank after a cold dawn, and they're left with a shelf of unopened plans, waiting for a clean restart that never comes.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Now the other one. Someone who believes the stool version. The same cold morning, and they moved the stool a foot. A try at the lock. The chart keeps going, and the gap is only a gap.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the best of the purpose note I keep for the next round, and you will not enjoy it, March.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I've got a comeback saved for later. It isn't kind, and you'll hear it when you're not braced.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Here's where I land. What broke the plan was the story told about the missed hour, the blank square that made the whole chart look finished.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the stool was the plan all along, and I offer J the title Keeper of the Unfinished Chart, in its honour.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: No. But you're right about the stool. Now the mug, which I'm moving an inch as we speak.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Up next, the rest of the chain and the purpose note, where the nasty bit lives.

segments.title: THE KETTLE THAT WAS ALREADY WARM
segments.angle: How might I look at this problem from an entirely different perspective?

sources.text: Consistency Compounds Exponentially: The real opportunity cost is who you would be and what you would have IF you were able to remain 100% consistent in your routine.
Staying On Your Purpose: Don't wait any longer. Don't believe the myth that "one day, things will be different". They won't.
Staying On Your Purpose: Spend at least 1 hour a day doing what you feel you're meant to do, now.
Staying On Your Purpose: Men who have lived significant lives are men who never waited
Consistency Compounds Exponentially: Allowing your consistency to break sets you back magnitudes more than you could ever imagine.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A kettle climbing toward the boil, a mug that isn't quite square on its tile, and the thought you've had a hundred times: once the week settles, I'll properly start. Hold that. The purpose note has no patience for it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Most people reckon tomorrow'll be different once things calm down. Quieter life, kinder mornings, and then the real start. It sounds sensible. I'd have signed up over breakfast.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Sensible! A noble sentiment, March. Tomorrow is the sunrise every great man keeps in his pocket, waiting on the tide to turn of its own accord. I have never once seen the tide oblige.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the waiting's the trap. Not the calm.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The note says it plainly. 'Don't wait any longer.' Then it kills the myth outright: 'Don't believe the myth that "one day, things will be different". They won't.' I'd have that framed above the hearth.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: They won't. Fine. Test it on a Tuesday.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Say it's still dark, and you're the one putting the water on. You think, I'll do the hour once the week's easier. The water clicks off, and the hour's still sat there, untouched, looking at you...

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the man has merely been sensible. There's nothing wrong with a kettle.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nothing wrong. Except it's the same decision Wednesday, and Thursday, and by the weekend it's a habit. The bad kind.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ah, now you arrive where the note wanted you. Hear its sharp claim: 'The real opportunity cost is who you would be and what you would have IF you were able to remain 100% consistent in your routine.'

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Who you'd be, not the hour.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Not one lost hour, March. A whole person, unbuilt. The lost hour is only the receipt.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the cost is the man you'd be in a year, not this morning.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Exactly the man. And worse, the man who stopped asking the question. The lost hour is the small print. The big purchase is who you never became, and no receipt returns that.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right. So I'm trying it on me. Dark still, water on, and I've decided today doesn't count because the week's too heavy. The brass key sits in the bowl by the tap, where it always sits.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A tragic little scene. Shall we have violins? Let me coach you. Tell the kettle it has a fine future, then return to bed like a heroine in a novel of ruin.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I'm not a heroine, I'm making tea. Smallest version. Kettle on. Stool moved one foot toward the lock. One try at the brass key. That's the whole thing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: One foot! Dear woman, a stool moved one foot is hardly a campaign. Call it what it is. Simple.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: One foot, yes.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Don't call it simple. People only say simple when they've already decided it's beneath them.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I said simple, and you bristle like a cat on a warm radiator. Very well. Not simple. Humble. A humble stool, with humble tea.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Humble's worse. Calling it anything small is a way of waiting. If it's simple you can skip it, and then call the skipping nothing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The tangent you've smuggled in under my nose. You name a small act simple, and in naming it you excuse yourself from doing it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Yes. And nobody starts something they've already written off. So the scorn is the waiting, dressed up for company.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A slow and hard truth, and I will not soften it for you. Contempt for the small thing is how a grand man waits his whole life for the great day, and never lifts the kettle.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ouch. Fair.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Harsher than mine. Good. Back to the stool. The dark start, the try at the lock, and the chart's got a blank square where the day should be.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A broken square. The streak has ended. What use is one try at a lock when the run is already over?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The try keeps the gap a gap. One blank square, not a verdict. Next time the water's on, and the chart reads one miss, not a finished plan.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now the halves meet, and I believe I see it at last. 'They won't' says the different tomorrow never comes. The consistency note says the cost is who you'd have become. Side by side, the day you wait is the very day your compounding stops.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So waiting is where the growth stops compounding.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Neither note shows it alone, March. The purpose note cries wait no longer, the consistency note tallies the loss, but only together do they show a wait is a withdrawal from your future, made in your own name.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Withdrawal. Noted.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A withdrawal. Okay, I'll allow the word. Now the fork. Picture someone who believes the purpose note.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Their Tuesday is ordinary. Water on before the blanket wins. The key gets tried once. The chart keeps one gap, and it doesn't read as a verdict on the whole plan. Nothing heroic. Just the next day, arriving on time.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And now the sharpest line of the purpose note, which I have kept back, March, until you finally stopped talking. 'Men who have lived significant lives are men who never waited.' Significant! That's the whole of it, in one breath.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right, and that's the stool again, wearing a bigger coat.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A bigger coat, yes. And I offer J a title to go with it: Lord of the Early Hour. Grand, is it not? A crown for a man who makes his tea before dawn.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: No. He doesn't need a crown for making tea. Warden of the Early Brew, though? That sounds like a pub sign.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then Warden it shall be, though I suspect you've simply picked the least flattering crown in the room.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Least flattering fits a kettle. Back to the start. The cold open, the mug one inch off true, the week that was going to settle.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Tomorrow won't be the day it changes. The kettle's already warm, and the stool's already moved.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Yes, March, you were right, and I shall say it only once, in the small hours, where no one can hold me to it. Tomorrow is a myth, and the kettle is already warm. Unbearably right, which I will forgive by morning.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Up next, Learning: Best Practices and The Present Moment Is All That Exists. Bring the kettle.
